title: Fast Fallbacks: Sales Sprint Deck (WIP)
content:
Slide 1 — Title
Fast Fallbacks: Short sprint deck for field sellers
Speaker note: one-page, 10-min run, focus on how we keep apps online when load spikes or models degrade. emphasize reliability without heavy ops lift.

Slide 2 — Purpose & context
- Purpose: Give sellers and solutions engineers a compact narrative and demo flow to show effective fallback strategies using Redwood routing and model variants.
- Context: Many prospects worry about model regressions, variable latency during peak, and cost spikes. This deck shows an operational story — not deep infra.
- Use: 10–12 min live demo + 5 min Q&A, appendix for technical deep-dive.

Slide 3 — Core selling thesis (soundbite)
- "Keep your app responsive and predictable: graceful model fallbacks that protect latency, cost, and business flows."
- Quick investor-style bulleted proof points:
  - Automatic routing preserves 95th-pctl latency during overloaded windows in our customer benchmarks.
  - Route-level canaries allow rollback without downtime.
  - Cost-aware policies reduce per-token spend by 12–35% on mixed workloads.

Slide 4 — Typical buyer worries (talk tracks per persona)
- Platform engineer: "How do I keep SLAs when model performance changes?" -> talk about routing policies, capacity tiers, and dedicated pools.
- ML engineer: "Will fallbacks change output semantics?" -> talk about model variant mapping, prompt-preserving wrappers, and eval gates.
- Product/PO: "Will our UX break if model changes?" -> mention A/B rollouts + canary thresholds + automatic fallback to cached responses for common prompts.

Slide 5 — High-level architecture (1-slide diagram, speaker text)
- Components to call out: API layer, smart-router, model catalog (variants/quantized), dedicated pool, KV cache, metrics + rollback controller.
- Speaker note: keep diagram simple — boxes and arrows. call out where policy decisions live (routing config in Console).

Slide 6 — Fallback patterns (practical examples for field)
- Pattern A: Latency-first route -> prefer low-latency quantized variant, fallback to cached prefix for repeated prompts.
- Pattern B: Quality-preserving route -> attempt full-precision model, fallback to smaller model + post-rerank if threshold fail.
- Pattern C: Cost-control route -> prefer cheapest compatible variant during non-critical traffic, escalate during paid conversions.
- Each pattern: 1-sentence business benefit + 1-sentence technical implementation.

Slide 7 — Demo script (5–7 minutes)
- Start: show Console route config (policy: latency_p95 < 500ms, quality_threshold=0.82) -> quickly toggle to simulate overloaded pools (throttle).
- Show: automatic routing to fallback variant and preserved API surface -> make a single API call and stream response showing shorter latencies.
- Show: telemetry panel -> token cost drop, latency p95 stabilized, event log shows fallback triggered and rollback decisions.
- Finish: flip canary to force A/B with user group -> show no downtime and controlled traffic shift.

Slide 8 — Battlecard: common objections + rebuttals (quick lines)
- "We just host our own models." -> "Self-hosting is fine; Redwood standardizes routing, rollback, and canary policies across environments — you get predictable SLOs without engineering sprints."
- "Fallback will change outputs and break UX." -> "We map variants with prompt-preserving wrappers, precomputed reranking, and built-in eval checks. For high-sensitivity flows we recommend conservative canary bandwidth + human-in-loop gating."
- "Costs will spike with extra traffic during failover." -> "Routing is policy-aware: cost caps + priority queues ensure failover stays within configured budget; we also offer burst capacity contracts for predictable charge."

Slide 9 — Quick competitor delta (talking bullets, avoid naming specific vendors in slides; use 'other endpoints')
- Redwood: unified routing + per-route canaries + integrated KV caching + policy editor in Console.
- Other endpoints: simple single-tier endpoints, manual rollbacks, less transparent cost attribution.
- Field note: when asked for specifics, pull the 'differentiators cheat sheet' from appendix.

Slide 10 — Pricing & procurement talking points
- Hosted API: usage + small premium for advanced routing features; emphasize fast time-to-value.
- Dedicated: reserved capacity commitment reduces unit price, includes SLA that covers routing failover behavior.
- Private: enterprise licensing for air-gapped or regulated customers — includes optional on-prem orchestration for fallbacks.
- Negotiation tip: offer a 3-month pilot with reduced reserved capacity and an ops workshop to tune policies; use PRO Service SKU as an upsell.

Slide 11 — Tactical checklist for SE during discovery
- Ask about: current latency p95, error modes during peak, top-50 prompts, SLAs expected, existing caching/batching heuristics.
- Collect: sample prompt set (top 200), traffic curve for last 30 days, current failover plan.
- SE play: recommend one of the three patterns above and propose a 2-week pilot.

Slide 12 — Appendix: technical deep-dive pointers
- Config knobs: routing priority, quality thresholds (0.0–1.0), cost caps, canary ramp schedule, cache TTLs.
- Safety: KMS keys + audit logs supported in Private and Dedicated.
- Telemetry: per-token cost breakdown, route-level tracing, sample diffs for fallback-triggered responses.
- Links: Confluence playbook (internal) and a short checklist for SRE handoff.

Slide 13 — Unresolved / TODO (notes to self)
- Add small chart that shows token-cost delta for a realistic ecommerce triage (pre-computed numbers).
- Flesh out 'quality-preserving' example with real prompt and two model outputs to demo semantic parity.
- Get approval from legal on the procurement bullet language for pilot offers.
- Confirm whether dedicated pool SLA verbiage can be used in public slides.

Slide 14 — Closing / call to action
- CTA: "Run a 2-week failover pilot: we configure routing, run canaries, and show delta vs current baseline."
- Next steps for AE/SE: open GTMSUP-482 (linked) to request a pilot pack and schedule a 60-min tune session.

Notes section (freeform, for SE):
- Keep demo script under 7 minutes. Practise toggling policy switches — UI delay is ~2s.
- If prospect asks about model drift detection: point to Optimize product features and the evals harness.
- If prospect is AWS-native and mentions VPC peering: surface Private deployment option + on-prem package note.
- Short hand-offs to SRE: include request id and sample prompt set; attach Telemetry export (CSV) to the ticket.

End of deck.

Metadata: created as lightweight field kit for AE/SE to run short proof points in discovery. Heavily iterative. Keep small, link to the longer 'fallbacks playbook' on Confluence when a deep dive is requested.
